title: The queue you're standing in, you helped build.
subtitle: Arrival windows, screening throughput, terminal capacity. None of it malice, all of it arithmetic.

text: Your arrival window is not a suggestion, it is the schedule.
sub: Terminals stagger arrivals because screening has a fixed throughput. Everyone turning up at eleven to be first aboard is precisely what produces the two-hour line at eleven.

title: Four things that shorten your day

items.head: Arrive inside your window, not before
items.body: The later half of your slot is usually the quietest part of the whole morning.

items.head: Fly in the day before. Always.
items.body: The missed-embarkation cases that end worst are flight-delay cases, not late-tour cases.

items.head: Know the initial-boarding rule
items.body: It is stricter than a port day. Royal Caribbean, for one, requires guests aboard no less than an hour before departure.

items.head: Read the first daily programme on deck
items.body: All-aboard times for day two, and the port agent's details. Read it with a drink, not in the cabin.

left.label: Rushed
items: Queue in a lounge from six

right.label: Unhurried
items: A night ashore at the far end

text: The cheapest flight of the trip is what usually costs the most.
sub: A same-day arrival saves a hotel night and risks the entire fare. I have never once regretted booking a client into the embarkation port the evening before.

quote: Two nights of hotel — one at each end — is the least glamorous money you will spend, and the best insured.

title: Send this to whoever books the flights
body: That is where the risk lives. Tell me your embarkation port and sail date and I'll say plainly whether the flight you're holding is one I'd let a client fly.
